title: Fixing Activation Before You Touch Acquisition
transcript:
Jordan Vance: Today I'm talking with Priya Chandrasekaran, who led growth for two Series B SaaS companies before starting her own consultancy. Priya, everyone wants to talk about acquisition channels. You told me before we started recording that most teams are solving the wrong problem. Why?

Priya Chandrasekaran: Because if your activation rate is broken, every new acquisition channel you turn on just pours more water into a leaky bucket. I've seen teams triple their ad spend and their net new active users barely move, because seventy percent of signups never reach the moment where the product actually delivers value. The fix isn't a bigger funnel. It's a narrower, faster path to what I call the first honest win.

Jordan Vance: What's a first honest win?

Priya Chandrasekaran: It's the first time a user experiences the core value of the product with their own real data, not a demo or a sample workspace. For a project management tool, that's not signing up, it's not even creating a project. It's the moment they see their own task move from not-done to done and get a small hit of relief. Everything before that moment is friction. Everything after it is retention work.

Jordan Vance: How do you find where teams are losing people before that moment?

Priya Chandrasekaran: I pull the signup-to-first-honest-win funnel and I look for the single biggest drop-off step. Almost always it's one of three things: an empty state that gives the user no obvious next action, a setup flow that asks for information the user doesn't have yet, like inviting teammates before they've decided the tool is worth it, or a required integration step that has external dependencies, like connecting a calendar or a data source, before the user has seen any value at all. If you make people configure before they experience, you lose them.

Jordan Vance: What's the fix?

Priya Chandrasekaran: Sequence experience before configuration. Give people a pre-populated example, or auto-generate their first project from a two-question quiz, so they see the payoff first. Then let them redo it with their real data once they're already sold. We did this at my last company for a scheduling product. We used to ask new users to connect their calendar, set their availability rules, and invite a client before they saw anything. We flipped it: we generated a fake demo booking page instantly, let them experience booking a slot as if they were a customer, and only asked for calendar connection once they clicked publish on their own page. Signup-to-first-honest-win went from seventeen percent to forty-four percent in six weeks.

Jordan Vance: That's a huge jump. Was there a tradeoff?

Priya Chandrasekaran: Yes, support load went up temporarily because more people reached the real setup step and had questions about it, which is actually a good problem. You're moving your drop-off later in the funnel, closer to genuine product questions instead of losing people to confusion before they even understood what the product does. The team has to be ready for that shift in where the friction shows up.

Jordan Vance: If someone listening only does one thing this week, what should it be?

Priya Chandrasekaran: Write down, in one sentence, what your first honest win is. Not your onboarding checklist, the actual moment of value. Then pull your funnel data and find the single step right before that moment with the worst conversion. Fix only that step before you touch anything else. Most teams try to fix five steps at once and can't tell what worked.
